sentences.text: The genus Parahelicoprion contains two species: P. clerci from Russia and P. mariosuarezi from Bolivia. Both species share tooth crowns with long, backwards-sweeping recessed lower sections and curved denticles along their edges.

The holotype of Parahelicoprion clerci measures 25 cm (10 inches) in profile and includes six articulated tooth crowns plus a smaller fragment. The upper tips of Parahelicoprion tooth crowns are uniquely rounded and blunt, unlike the pointed tips of many related edestoids. The form of the serrations and crenulations on Parahelicoprion teeth is unique to this species.
Parahelicoprion mariosuarezi preserves a denticle-bearing parasymphyseal tooth near the midline of the mouth, a type not found in P. clerci.
The genus Parahelicoprion was formally described by Karpinsky in 1924.
Parahelicoprion mariosuarezi was described by Merino-Rodo and Janvier in 1986.
The type specimen of P. clerci was found in the Ural Mountains of Russia in Artinskian strata. The holotype of Parahelicoprion clerci was prepared and assembled by Karpinsky in 1916.
The holotype of P. clerci consists of tooth fragments that were damaged by mining and broken into pieces.

Parahelicoprion was a carnivore that lived in marine environments. It has been suggested that Parahelicoprion was the apex predator of its ecosystem, with its serrated tooth whorl adapted for cutting prey.
It is hypothesized that members of the Helicoprionidae were molluscivorous, feeding primarily on ammonoid and coleoid cephalopods.

Like other family members, the teeth of Parahelicoprion angle forward in the mouth. Parahelicoprion teeth increase significantly in size toward the rear of the whorl. Parahelicoprion teeth farthest forward are rounder and more asymmetrical than the nearly symmetrical rear teeth.
The rear edges of the frontmost tooth crowns in Parahelicoprion form sharp, non-serrated cutting blades. In the rear tooth crowns of Parahelicoprion, both the front and rear edges are blade-like.

Due to incomplete fossils, estimates of Parahelicoprion's size and ecology are speculative, though it is assumed to have been large, predatory, and potentially pelagic. Karpinsky suggested Parahelicoprion clerci was very large to accommodate its significantly larger tooth crowns compared to Helicoprion. Richard Ellis estimated Parahelicoprion was at least 100 feet long, unless it had a gigantic head or oversized teeth. Non-academic sources suggest Parahelicoprion lengths of 11-13 meters, but these are not supported by scientific literature.

Parahelicoprion belongs to the family Helicoprionidae within the order Eugeneodontiformes. The family Helicoprionidae is defined by possessing tooth whorls with forward-angled, blade-like tooth crowns and often completely fused tooth roots.
The type species of the genus Parahelicoprion is Helicoprion clerci.

Parahelicoprion lived during the Early Permian, with the latest known occurrence in the Artinskian stage and an assumed extinction by the end of the Cisuralian; however, one estimate places it between 298.9 and 293.52 million years ago during the Asselian stage.
Authors have suggested P. mariosuarezi had a short tooth whorl at the tip of elongated jaws, but acknowledged the material is too fragmentary for confident comparison.
It is debated whether crushing teeth similar to Campodus or Orodus were present in Parahelicoprion, as no other teeth are confidently associated with the species.
Estimates of Parahelicoprion's total body size are controversial despite its large tooth crowns.
Karpinsky suggested that the extinction of Uralian edestoids like Parahelicoprion was caused by the disappearance of the seaway connecting the Arctic and Tethys oceans.
